name: Galena kohl

card.summary: A black eye cosmetic made from ground galena (lead sulfide), worn since antiquity to define and darken the eyes.
card.note: Lead-based kohl is considered unsafe by the US FDA, which bars its import and sale.

quick.overview:
Galena kohl is a dark powder or paste made from lead sulfide, applied around and inside the eyelids as eyeliner. It makes the eyes look larger, darker and more defined, an effect used from ancient Egypt to present-day South Asia.

Traditional kohl was also made from stibnite or soot. Egyptian eye paint often used galena as black on the upper lids and green malachite below, and kohl was believed to protect the eyes as well as adorn them.
quick.how: Kohl is traditionally applied with a small stick or fingertip along the lash line or waterline. Modern eyeliners in Western markets usually use carbon or charcoal instead of galena.
quick.risks: Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to raised blood lead levels, with complications including anemia and developmental problems in children. The US FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe.

lead: Galena kohl is eye makeup made from lead sulfide. It has been used to outline and darken the eyes, giving a bold, defined look, and has been worn in Egypt since the Naqada III era, about 3100 BCE, by people of all classes [1].

Besides appearance, wearers believed it shielded the eyes from sun and the evil eye, and the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) describes kohl compounds as protective [1]. Traditional kohl was often stibnite (antimony sulfide); galena-based versions are common in modern surma [1].
Studies and regulators have raised concern about lead exposure from such products [1].

chain: Dark mineral powder along lash line
angle.text: Applied to the lids and waterline, kohl darkens the rim of the eye so the eyes read as bigger and sharper. Egyptians paired black galena above the eye with green malachite below.

infobox: Not an approved color additive; import and sale illegal [1]

paras: Traditional kohl was made by crushing stibnite. Egyptian eye paint often used galena as black for the upper lids and malachite as green for the lower. Indian kajal is traditionally lamp soot mixed with oils, sometimes with camphor or sandalwood. Surma is a South Asian cosmetic made from galena or other minerals [1].

Lead isotope analysis of kohl from Lower Nubian cemeteries, c. 2300 to 1500 BCE, suggests Nubians used and perhaps produced it [1]. Hatshepsut, an 18th Dynasty pharaoh, had charred frankincense ground into kohl, the first recorded use of that resin (c. 1500 BCE) [1].

No studies found on cosmetic effect. Research on kohl has examined lead content: early-1990s analyses found lead as high as 84 percent in some commercial kohl, and a later study of Egyptian and Indian kohl found lead in about a third of samples. Findings on blood lead are mixed, with some studies not finding a link [1]. A 2010 French study linked low concentrations of lead compounds to increased nitric oxide production, and an older test found inhibition of some bacteria [1].

Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to higher blood lead levels; complications of lead poisoning include anemia, developmental delay and convulsions. A 2016 Pakistani study found lead in the nails of many pregnant women, with surma a likely source. The FDA does not list kohl among approved color additives and bars its importation and sale in the US [1].
